unit.title: Apply the principles of contract law

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which list gives the essential elements of a valid contract?
options: Offer, acceptance, consideration, intention, capacity
Offer, invoice, receipt, delivery note and payment
Quotation, purchase order, signature and company stamp
Advertisement, enquiry, discussion and a handshake

questions.stem: A Half Way Tree electronics store displays a television in its window with a price label of J$85,000. In contract law, what is the price label?
options: A binding offer to sell to the first buyer
A contract that is made once someone sees it
An invitation to treat
A form of consideration from the store

questions.stem: A supplier emails a hotel: 'We will supply 200 bath towels at J$1,200 each, delivered by 1 March.' What is this email most likely to be?
options: A general advertisement to the public
An offer that the hotel may accept
A contract that already binds both sides
An invitation to treat with no legal effect

questions.stem: The hotel replies: 'We accept, but at J$1,000 a towel.' What is the legal effect of this reply?
options: It forms a contract at J$1,000 a towel
It forms a contract at J$1,200 a towel
It forms a contract at an average price
It is a counter-offer that rejects the offer

questions.stem: When is an offer usually accepted?
options: When agreement to all its terms is communicated
When the offeree privately decides to accept it
When the offeree starts to read the terms
When the offeror sends a reminder about it

questions.stem: A supplier writes: 'If we do not hear from you by Friday, we will treat this as your order.' The buyer does not reply. Is there a contract?
options: Yes, because the buyer had a full week to reply
Yes, because the supplier set a clear deadline
No, because silence is not usually acceptance
No, because the letter was not signed by hand

questions.stem: A seller offers a used van to Mr Barnes and promises to keep the offer open for a week, but Mr Barnes pays nothing for that promise. On day three, before he accepts, the seller tells him the offer is withdrawn. What is the position?
options: The seller must keep the offer open for the full week
Mr Barnes may still accept and hold the seller to it
The seller must pay Mr Barnes for breaking the promise
The offer may be withdrawn before it is accepted

questions.stem: Under the general rule for acceptance by post, where post is a reasonable way to reply, when is the acceptance usually complete?
options: When the offeror opens and reads the letter
When the letter is properly posted
When the letter is delivered to the office
When the offeror replies to confirm it

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of consideration?
options: A thank-you card sent after a job was done
A hope that the other party will be pleased
A promise to pay J$50,000 for a service
A feeling of duty to help a neighbour out

questions.stem: After a contractor finished painting a church hall for free, the board promised to pay him J$40,000. It later refused to pay. Why may the promise not be enforceable?
options: The work was done before the promise
Churches cannot make binding contracts
J$40,000 is too small a sum to be enforced
The painter did not do a good enough job

questions.stem: A firm sells an old printer to a staff member for J$1,000, far below its value. Is the contract valid?
options: No, because the price is far too low to count
No, because staff cannot contract with employers
No, because a fair price must be set by a valuer
Yes, as the price need not match the value

questions.stem: In a commercial agreement between two firms, what is usually presumed about their intention?
options: That they do not mean to be legally bound
That they intend to be legally bound
That only a signed deed can bind them
That the larger firm alone is bound

questions.stem: Two sisters agree that one will cook Sunday dinner if the other does the washing up. What does the law usually presume?
options: They do not intend legal relations
They have made a binding service contract
Either can sue the other for breach
The agreement must be put in writing

questions.stem: Which party is most likely to lack full capacity to make a binding contract?
options: A sole trader buying stock for her shop
A company acting through its directors
A 15-year-old buying a car on credit
A retired teacher buying a fridge for cash

questions.stem: Before signing a large contract with a company, why should a manager check who is signing on its behalf?
options: To decide which person to invite to lunch
To find out that person's personal income
To check that person's school record
To confirm the person has authority to bind it

questions.stem: An agreement for building materials says the price 'will be agreed later', with no way of working it out. What is the main risk?
options: It will be binding at the highest market price
It may be too uncertain to be binding
It must be approved by a court first
It will become binding after one month

questions.stem: What is the main reason to put an important business contract in writing even when the law does not require it?
options: To give clear evidence of the agreed terms
To make it legal, as spoken contracts never are
To avoid paying any GCT on the contract
To let one party change the terms later

questions.stem: What are the terms called that the parties themselves have stated and agreed, in writing or by word of mouth?
options: Implied terms
Collateral warranties
Express terms
Exclusion clauses

questions.stem: A Mandeville shop sells a kettle that will not heat water. The receipt says nothing about quality. What mainly protects the buyer?
options: Nothing, as the receipt is silent on quality
Only any promise the cashier made out loud
A refund only if the box is still unopened
Terms implied by law on quality and fitness

questions.stem: A Negril hotel agrees to host a wedding reception on a set date, then double-books and cannot host it on that date. What has the hotel broken?
options: A warranty, giving a right to damages only
A condition, so the couple may end the contract
An implied term that has no legal effect
No term, as the date was only a target

questions.stem: A supplier delivers the right office chairs on time, but in a slightly different shade of grey from the one ordered. Which remedy is most likely?
options: Ending the whole contract and returning the chairs
A court order forcing the supplier to repaint
Damages for any loss, with the contract kept
Criminal charges against the supplier

questions.stem: When is an exclusion clause, limiting a party's liability, most likely to form part of a contract?
options: When it was made clear before agreement
When it is printed on a receipt given afterwards
When it is hidden in very small print
When one party mentions it after a loss

questions.stem: A seller tells a buyer that a delivery van has done 40,000 km, knowing it has done 140,000 km. The buyer relies on this and buys it. What can the buyer usually seek?
options: Nothing, as buyers should always check
Only an apology from the seller
A second van at no extra cost
To set the contract aside and claim damages

questions.stem: A supplier threatens to damage a manager's property unless she signs a contract. What is the effect on the contract?
options: It is fully binding, as she signed it
It may be set aside because of duress
It is binding once the goods arrive
It is binding unless a court is told at once

questions.stem: A businessman agrees to pay a public officer to speed up a permit. What is the status of that agreement?
options: Valid, as long as the payment is receipted
Valid, if the permit is actually issued
Illegal and unenforceable
Binding, but only on the public officer

questions.stem: As a general rule, who can enforce the terms of a contract?
options: The parties to it
Anyone who might benefit from it
Any member of the public
The government agency in that area

questions.stem: Two weeks before the agreed delivery date, a supplier tells a firm that it will not deliver at all. What is this?
options: A minor breach of a warranty term
A lawful change of the contract
Frustration of the whole contract
An anticipatory breach of contract

questions.stem: What is the main aim of damages for breach of contract?
options: To punish the party that broke the contract
To put the injured party where performance would have
To share the loss equally between both parties
To give the court a fee for hearing the case

questions.stem: A caterer cancels a J$450,000 contract for a conference lunch a week before the event. The organiser hires another caterer for J$520,000. Ignoring other costs, what damages would the organiser normally claim?
A courier delivers a machine part late. Unknown to the courier, the delay stops the customer's whole factory. Why might the courier not have to pay for the lost output?
options: The loss was not foreseeable when they contracted
Couriers can never be sued for late delivery
Factories must always keep spare parts in stock
The customer did not pay the courier in advance

questions.stem: A tenant breaks a shop lease and moves out early. What is the landlord expected to do about its loss?
options: Leave the shop empty and claim the full rent
Raise the rent for the next tenant to cover it
Sell the tenant's goods left in the shop
Take reasonable steps to find a new tenant

questions.stem: In which case is a court most likely to order specific performance?
options: A contract to buy 50 cases of bottled water
A contract to buy a particular piece of land
A contract to hire a band for a party
A contract to buy standard office paper

questions.stem: A former distributor keeps selling goods under the firm's brand after its contract ended, against the contract's terms. Which remedy would stop this?
options: Rescission
Specific performance
An injunction
Liquidated damages

questions.stem: A building contract sets liquidated damages of J$40,000 for each day of late completion. The building is finished 9 days late. How much can the owner claim?
Why might a court refuse to enforce a very large 'late fee' written into a contract?
options: Late fees may never appear in a contract
The fee was agreed by both parties in writing
The fee was written in the contract in J$
It is a penalty, far above any genuine loss

questions.stem: Two firms agree to end their service contract early on terms they both accept. How is the contract discharged?
options: By frustration
By agreement
By breach
By performance

questions.stem: A hotel contracts to host a conference, but the building is destroyed by fire, through no one's fault, before the date. What is the likely legal position?
options: The hotel must pay full damages to the organiser
The organiser must still pay the full price
The contract is frustrated and both are released
The hotel must host it at another hotel

questions.stem: A project manager wants to change the scope of work under a signed contract. What is the best practice?
options: Agree a written variation signed by both
Tell the contractor by phone and carry on
Make the change and pay less at the end
Ask the site staff to change it quietly

questions.stem: Which practice best helps a manager avoid disputes while a contract is being carried out?
options: Wait until the end to check the work
Keep all problems quiet to keep good relations
Pay early so that the other side is happy
Keep records, monitor work and raise issues early

questions.stem: Two firms in a contract dispute want a private, quick process in which a neutral person helps them reach their own agreement. Which method fits?
options: A full court trial
Mediation
Arbitration with a binding award
A complaint to the newspaper

questions.stem: A contract says that disputes must go to a neutral expert whose decision will bind both parties. What is this method called?
options: Negotiation
Mediation
Arbitration
Conciliation

questions.stem: Before signing a supply contract, what should a manager do first?
options: Read every term and get advice where unsure
Sign it quickly before the supplier changes it
Ask the supplier to explain it and rely on that
Check only the price and the delivery date

questions.stem: A customer accepts a firm's online terms by clicking 'I agree'. Can this form a contract?
options: No, only signed paper contracts are valid
No, unless a lawyer witnesses the click
Only for purchases under J$10,000
Yes, if the terms were available and agreed

questions.stem: Why should a manager read a supplier's standard terms printed on the back of a quotation?
options: They are there for decoration only
They may become part of the contract
They apply only if signed by a lawyer
They are always the same for every firm

questions.stem: A Kingston business sells goods to the public. Which kind of law gives buyers rights that the firm's own terms cannot take away?
options: Company law
Intellectual property law
Consumer protection law
Employment law

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one-word term names a statement of willingness to be bound on certain terms, which becomes a contract once it is accepted?
What one-word term names the thing of value, such as money, goods or a service, that each party gives in return for the other's promise?
What three-word term names a catalogue, price list or shop display that invites people to make an offer?
What term names a reply that changes the terms of an offer and so rejects the original offer?
A buyer ordered 300 chairs at J$4,200 each. The seller failed to deliver, and the buyer bought the same chairs elsewhere at J$4,650 each. What price difference can the buyer usually claim, in J$?
What two-word term names a sum fixed in a contract in advance, as a genuine estimate of loss, to be paid if a party breaks a term such as a completion date?
What two-word term names a contract term that excludes or limits one party's liability?
What two-word term names a court order that requires a party to carry out its contract, used where money would not be enough?
What one-word term names a person's legal ability to enter into a binding contract?
What one-word term names the duty of an injured party to take reasonable steps to reduce its loss after a breach?
What one-word term names a major term that goes to the root of a contract, whose breach allows the innocent party to end the contract?
What one-word term names a minor term in a contract whose breach gives a right to damages only?
What one-word term names a false statement of fact that persuades a party to enter into a contract?
What one-word term names the ending of a contract when an unforeseen event, which is no one's fault, makes it impossible to perform?
A buyer pays a deposit of 30% on a contract worth J$2,400,000. What balance is due on delivery, in J$?

essays.stem: Explain the essential elements of a valid contract, using as an example an agreement for a Kingston hardware supplier to provide materials to a building contractor.
essays.modelAnswer: First, there must be an offer: a clear statement of terms by which the maker is willing to be bound, such as the supplier's quotation for 500 bags of cement at a set price, delivered on a set date. A price list or advertisement is usually only an invitation to treat. Second, there must be acceptance: the contractor's unconditional agreement to those exact terms, communicated to the supplier. A reply that changes the terms is a counter-offer, not acceptance. Third, there must be consideration: each side gives something of value, here the materials in return for payment. Fourth, both parties must intend to create legal relations, which is presumed in business agreements like this one. Fifth, both must have capacity; for a company, the person signing must have authority to bind it. In addition, the terms must be certain enough to enforce, such as the quantity, price and delivery date, the agreement must be for a lawful purpose, and it must be made freely, without misrepresentation or pressure. If all these are present, a binding contract exists, whether it is in writing or not, although writing gives better evidence.
markingPoints: Offer, distinguished from an invitation to treat
Unconditional acceptance communicated; counter-offer explained
Consideration on both sides
Intention to create legal relations and capacity, including authority
Certainty, legality and genuine consent, applied to the example

essays.stem: On Monday, a supplier emails a contractor offering 500 bags of cement at J$1,450 a bag, open until Friday. On Tuesday, the contractor replies, 'We will take 500 at J$1,350.' On Wednesday, the supplier says it cannot lower the price. On Thursday, the contractor emails, 'Fine, we accept your offer at J$1,450.' Analyse whether, and when, a contract was formed.
essays.modelAnswer: Monday's email is an offer: it sets out clear terms, the goods, quantity and price, and states it is open until Friday. Tuesday's reply is not an acceptance, because it changes the price. It is a counter-offer, which rejects the original offer and brings it to an end. The supplier is now the party receiving an offer, at J$1,350. On Wednesday, the supplier rejects the counter-offer by saying it cannot lower the price. It does not renew its original offer; it simply refuses the new terms. On Thursday, the contractor tries to accept the Monday offer at J$1,450. Because that offer was ended by the counter-offer, there is nothing left to accept, even though Friday has not arrived. The Thursday email is therefore a new offer by the contractor to buy at J$1,450. No contract is formed unless the supplier accepts this new offer, for example by confirming the order or by delivering the cement. In practice, the contractor should ask the supplier to confirm in writing so that both sides are clear that a contract exists and on what terms.
markingPoints: Monday email is an offer
Tuesday reply is a counter-offer that ends the original offer
Wednesday is a rejection, not a renewed offer
Thursday email is a new offer, so no contract yet
Contract only when the supplier accepts; advises written confirmation

essays.stem: Explain the difference between express and implied terms, and between conditions and warranties, and why the difference matters when a term is broken.
essays.modelAnswer: Express terms are those the parties actually state and agree, in writing or orally, such as the price, delivery date and specification. Implied terms are not stated but are included by law or by the circumstances, for example that goods sold by a business are of acceptable quality and fit for their purpose, or terms so obvious that both parties must have intended them. Terms also differ in importance. A condition is a major term that goes to the root of the contract, such as the date of a wedding reception or the type of machine ordered. If a condition is broken, the innocent party may treat the contract as ended and also claim damages. A warranty is a minor term, such as the exact shade of a product's colour or a small detail of packaging. If a warranty is broken, the innocent party may claim damages for any loss but must still carry out its own side of the contract. The difference matters because ending a contract for breach of a warranty would itself be a breach. Managers should therefore state clearly in contracts which terms are essential.
markingPoints: Express terms defined with examples
Implied terms by law or circumstances
Condition and the right to end the contract
Warranty and the right to damages only
Why the difference matters and stating essential terms clearly

essays.stem: A supplier fails to deliver 500 bags of cement ordered at J$1,450 a bag. The contractor buys the same cement elsewhere at J$1,620 a bag and pays J$12,000 extra in transport. It also claims J$600,000 profit lost on a separate project the supplier knew nothing about. Calculate the damages the contractor is likely to recover, and explain the principles involved.
essays.modelAnswer: The aim of damages is to put the contractor in the position it would have been in if the contract had been performed. The extra cost of the replacement cement is J$1,620 − J$1,450 = J$170 a bag, so 500 × J$170 = J$85,000. The extra transport cost of J$12,000 arose naturally from having to buy elsewhere, so it is likely to be recoverable too, giving J$85,000 + J$12,000 = J$97,000. The claim for J$600,000 lost profit on the separate project is unlikely to succeed. Damages cover losses that arise naturally from the breach, or that both parties could reasonably have foreseen when they made the contract. The supplier knew nothing about the other project, so this loss is probably too remote. The contractor also had a duty to mitigate its loss, which it did by buying replacement cement quickly. If it had waited and prices had risen further, it might not recover the extra. The likely damages are therefore about J$97,000. The contractor should keep receipts and correspondence as evidence and first seek payment by letter or negotiation.
markingPoints: States the aim of damages
Calculates J$85,000 for the price difference
Adds J$12,000 transport: J$97,000
Lost profit on the other project is probably too remote
Explains mitigation and evidence

essays.stem: Compare damages, specific performance, injunction and rescission as remedies for problems with a contract, and say when each would be most suitable.
essays.modelAnswer: Damages are money paid to compensate the injured party for loss caused by a breach. They are the usual remedy and are available as of right once breach and loss are shown, but only for foreseeable losses and after reasonable steps to reduce the loss. They suit most commercial cases, such as late or missing deliveries of standard goods that can be bought elsewhere. Specific performance is a court order requiring a party to carry out the contract. It is discretionary and is used only where money would not be enough, usually because the subject is unique, such as a particular piece of land or a rare item. It is not usually ordered for contracts of personal service. An injunction is a court order to stop a party doing something, such as continuing to use a brand or breaking a confidentiality or exclusivity clause. Rescission sets the contract aside and returns the parties to where they were before, and is used where the contract was obtained by misrepresentation or pressure. The remedy should be chosen to fit the problem, and legal advice should be taken first.
markingPoints: Damages: purpose, limits and suitable cases
Specific performance: discretionary, for unique subject matter
Injunction: to stop a breach
Rescission: for misrepresentation or pressure
Matches remedy to situation

essays.stem: Explain how misrepresentation, duress, mistake and illegality can affect whether a contract is binding, with a business example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: A contract is binding only if both parties agree freely and on a true basis, for a lawful purpose. Misrepresentation is a false statement of fact that persuades someone to contract. If a seller says a delivery van has done 40,000 km when it has done 140,000 km, the buyer may be able to set the contract aside and, where the statement was careless or dishonest, claim damages. Duress is illegitimate pressure, such as threats to a person or their property, or improper economic threats, that forces someone to agree. A contract signed after a supplier threatens to damage a manager's car may be set aside. Mistake covers certain serious errors, such as both parties contracting for goods that, unknown to either of them, had already been destroyed. In such cases the contract may be void, although most ordinary mistakes, such as a poor bargain, do not affect it. Illegality arises where the purpose or performance breaks the law, such as an agreement to pay an officer for a permit. The courts will not enforce it. Managers should therefore check facts, avoid pressure and keep deals lawful.
markingPoints: Misrepresentation and its effect, with example
Duress and its effect, with example
Mistake in limited serious cases, with example
Illegality makes a contract unenforceable, with example
Links to genuine consent and lawful purpose

essays.stem: Plan the steps a manager should take before signing a two-year contract for security services at a Montego Bay hotel.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would define the hotel's needs clearly: the hours, number of guards, duties, standards and reporting, so the contract can be measured. I would follow the hotel's purchasing procedure to get competing quotations and check each bidder's licence, insurance, references and financial standing. When reviewing the draft contract, I would check that the parties are correctly named and that the person signing for the supplier has authority. I would check that the scope, service levels, price, payment terms and any price increases are clear and certain. I would look for important terms: who is liable for losses and injuries, insurance levels, confidentiality of guest information in line with the data protection law, staff screening, termination rights for poor service, notice periods and how disputes will be settled. I would watch for exclusion or limitation clauses that unfairly shift risk to the hotel, and for automatic renewal. I would negotiate changes in writing and get legal advice on anything unclear. Finally, I would make sure the contract is approved within my delegated authority, signed by both parties, and filed, with key dates recorded.
markingPoints: Defines needs and checks suppliers through proper procedure
Checks parties, authority and certainty of key terms
Reviews liability, insurance, confidentiality, termination and disputes
Watches for exclusion clauses and renewal; negotiates in writing and seeks advice
Approval within authority, signature and filing

essays.stem: Describe how a manager should manage a building contract while the work is being carried out, to prevent breaches and deal with changes.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager should start by summarising the contract's key obligations, dates, payment stages, quality standards and notice requirements, and sharing them with everyone involved. A named person should be responsible for the contract. Regular site meetings should be held with the contractor, with minutes that record progress, problems and agreed actions. The manager should check that work meets the specification before approving each payment and keep records, including photographs, inspection reports and correspondence. Problems should be raised in writing as soon as they appear, giving the contractor the chance to put them right, rather than storing them up until the end. Any change to the scope, price or timetable should be made by a written variation signed by both parties, with its effect on cost and time agreed before the work is done; informal instructions on site often lead to disputes. If delay occurs, the manager should check the contract's provisions, such as extensions of time and liquidated damages, and follow its notice steps. If a serious breach occurs, she should seek legal advice before ending the contract, because wrongly ending it could itself be a breach.
markingPoints: Summarises obligations and names a responsible person
Regular meetings, inspections and records
Raises problems early in writing
Changes by signed written variation
Uses contract provisions for delay and takes advice before ending it

essays.stem: Explain the main ways in which a contract can be discharged, and apply them to a resort whose contract to host an event is affected by a hurricane that damages the building.
essays.modelAnswer: A contract can be discharged in four main ways. The usual way is performance, when both parties do exactly what they promised. A contract can also be discharged by agreement, when the parties agree to end it or replace it, often with terms about refunds. It can be discharged by breach, when one party breaks a condition or refuses to perform and the other chooses to end the contract and claim damages. Finally, it can be discharged by frustration, when an event that neither party caused or could reasonably foresee makes performance impossible or radically different from what was agreed. If a hurricane damages the resort so badly that the event cannot be held on the agreed date, the contract may be frustrated, and both parties are released from future obligations. Money paid in advance may have to be returned, allowing for expenses already incurred, depending on the contract and the law. However, the contract may contain a clause on events beyond the parties' control, often called a force majeure clause, and this would usually decide the outcome. In practice, the parties may agree to move the event to a new date, discharging the original contract by agreement.
markingPoints: Performance
Agreement
Breach of a condition
Frustration explained and applied to the hurricane
Notes the effect of any force majeure clause and possible agreed rescheduling

essays.stem: A hotel and a building contractor disagree about defects in new guest rooms and about J$3,500,000 that the hotel is withholding. Evaluate negotiation, mediation, arbitration and court action, and recommend an approach.
essays.modelAnswer: Negotiation is direct discussion between the parties. It is cheap, private, quick and keeps the relationship, which matters if the contractor must still fix the defects. Its weakness is that it may fail if positions are fixed or trust is low. Mediation brings in a neutral mediator who helps both sides find their own settlement. It is still private and fairly low-cost, and often works where direct talks have stalled, but the mediator cannot impose a result. Arbitration uses a neutral arbitrator, often an expert in building, whose decision is binding. It is private and can be quicker than court, but it can be costly, and it is usually available only if the contract provides for it or both agree. Court action gives a binding, enforceable judgment and formal rules of evidence, but it is public, slow and expensive, and usually ends the relationship. I recommend starting with a structured negotiation supported by an independent inspection report on the defects. If that fails within an agreed period, the parties should try mediation. Arbitration or court should be kept as a last resort, following any dispute clause in the contract.
markingPoints: Negotiation: benefits and limits
Mediation: benefits and limits
Arbitration: binding, private, cost and contract basis
Court: binding but slow, public and costly
Justified, staged recommendation following any dispute clause

practical1.title: Review a draft supply contract and advise the manager
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up draft contract for a supplier to provide goods or services to a Jamaican organisation (for example cleaning supplies for a hotel group, or catering for a public agency's training centre), with the organisation's purchasing requirements. The draft contains gaps and risks, such as a missing delivery date, an unclear price, a wide exclusion clause, no termination right and no dispute clause. As a group, produce: a checklist confirming each element of a valid contract and whether it is present; a terms review table listing each important term, whether it is a condition or a warranty, its risk to the organisation and a suggested amendment; a marked-up copy of the draft showing the changes; and a one-page advice memo to the manager recommending whether to sign and what to negotiate first. Give each member a named role: lead reviewer (keeps time and writes the memo), formation checker (offer, acceptance, consideration, intention, capacity and authority), terms analyst, risks and remedies analyst (exclusion, liability, breach and remedies), and drafter (marks up the contract). In a group of four, the lead reviewer also marks up the contract. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Made-up draft contract and purchasing requirements from the assessor
Computers with word-processing software (track changes), and a printer
Highlighters, sticky notes and a flipchart
photos: The flipchart of contract elements and who is checking what
The advice memo to the manager
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Correctly identified which elements of a valid contract are present
Classified key terms sensibly as conditions or warranties
Found the main gaps and risks in the draft
Advice memo makes a reasoned recommendation in plain language
Kept the case confidential and stated that legal advice should be taken where needed
safety: Use only the made-up contract and invented names
Keep the case documents confidential to the group and the assessor
Give general principles only and do not present the work as formal legal advice
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Trace a contract's formation, calculate a breach claim and negotiate a settlement
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack of made-up emails and documents between a buyer and a supplier (for example a Kingston contractor and a hardware supplier), showing an offer, a counter-offer and later messages, followed by a late or failed delivery. As a group: build a timeline showing each message and its legal effect, and decide whether and when a contract was formed; calculate the damages the buyer could claim, using the figures in the pack, and note which losses are recoverable and why; draft a formal letter of claim; then hold a 20-minute role-played negotiation in which one pair acts for the buyer and another pair for the supplier, with a mediator chairing. Record the agreed settlement as a short written agreement signed by both sides. Give each member a named role: timeline analyst, damages calculator, letter writer, two negotiators (one for each side; in a group of four the timeline analyst also negotiates), and a mediator and note-taker played by the fifth member or the assessor. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack of made-up emails, quotations, delivery notes and invoices
Computers with word-processing and spreadsheet software
A meeting table set for four to five people
photos: The timeline on the flipchart, with the legal effect of each message
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Correctly identified the offer, counter-offer and acceptance, if any
Calculated the damages correctly and excluded losses that are too remote
Letter of claim is clear, factual and professional
Negotiated firmly but respectfully and looked for a workable settlement
Settlement is recorded clearly and signed by both sides
Explained the contract principles used when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up case and invented names
Keep the case and negotiation notes confidential
Behave respectfully in the role play and stop if anyone is uncomfortable
Present the work as a training exercise, not as legal advice
